note: Look, not law. Absorb or drop next sitting. A spark is not a trap.

items.claim: The gated 'seat packet' band measures seatPacket(root, null), the packet with no lane and so without the envelope: with F40 issued sizeBudget prints 99.7 per cent of 26 KB while packet.mjs seat F40 prints 31.6 KB.
items.whyNotLaw: Two readings, and the control plane could not settle it from the objects. Either the band measures a different object than the one that reaches a writer, which is D-59's family in the gate's own hand, or it is deliberately the byte-stable cacheable prefix at 26 with the envelope budgeted separately at 6, total about 32, in which case one label for two numbers 5.7 KB apart is what needs fixing. budgets.json's note and D-57 both speak of 'the packet' at 25.3 KB, which is the prefix reading. Settle it before the next ceiling argument: a control plane reading 99.7 per cent green can hand a seat 22 per cent more context than the number it just checked.

items.claim: A correction launch rebases the worktree (T81), which diverges the lane branch from its pushed tip, and 'push the branch only' does not authorise the force-with-lease that then needs.
items.whyNotLaw: Hit on F44's correction: the seat finished the work, was rejected non-fast-forward, correctly refused to rewrite a shared ref on its own authority and handed the call up. It was right to, and the cost was a stalled return the control plane finished by hand. T81's own remedy creates this, so the two belong together: a correction envelope should name the force-with-lease on its OWN lane branch as authorised, and say that main is never forced.

items.claim: The qwen seat keeps a memory store OUTSIDE git at ~/.qwen/memories, read into every later seat. Its note on this machine's bash first claimed the gate always reds 21, which is false; F47's seat found that at the objects and corrected it.
items.whyNotLaw: Two readings and the control plane cannot settle it from the objects. One: this is T50 and T26 with a new carrier. The fuse model says the repository is memory and a successor reads AGENTS, BOARD and its envelope and never a transcript, and sessions.json lists what a successor never reads. A store that survives session death and is injected into every later seat makes a fresh seat not fresh, sits in no packet, under no size budget, in no gate, and is reviewed by nobody. The false version of this very note would have been read as fact by every seat after it. Two: it demonstrably paid. F47's seat diagnosed the WSL launcher by the -e versus -c pair, which is what its own note taught, and it CORRECTED the note at the objects rather than trusting it. Measure before ruling: how many bytes reach a seat, whether they sit ahead of the byte-stable prefix and cost the 95 per cent cache hit measured on F47, and whether a note can be made a return the control plane reviews instead of a file nobody owns.

items.claim: The reviewer is a Claude subagent of the control-plane session, so it appears in NO seat census and writes NO row to any meter. Four reviews this sitting cost about 542000 subagent tokens and 188 tool uses, none of it reaching returns.json.
items.whyNotLaw: AGENTS section 3 is satisfied - never the author, never weaker than the writer, always a fresh session - and the reviews are paying for themselves, finding a blocking defect in three of four lanes this sitting. What is missing is accounting, and it has two edges the control plane cannot settle from the objects. The census reads the process table for harness processes, so a reviewer is invisible to the two-writer ceiling and to the dead-seat resume; that is arguably correct, since a reviewer is not a writer, but the census cannot CONFIRM it either way and a successor reading 0 running seats does not know whether a review is in flight. And the spend side is simply absent: writer spend is a row per lane read from the harness meter, while review spend exists only in a task notification this session will not outlive, so the factory's own record understates what a lane costs by however much its review cost. Measure before ruling: whether a subagent's usage can be read at all from this harness, and whether a review belongs in returns.json as its own row or as a field on the lane's row.

items.claim: Packet budgets measure total(parts) while the seat receives render(parts), which adds a header and blank line per part. F52: counted 32599, emitted 32705. The 106 unmeasured bytes leave 63 of real headroom where the tools imply 169.
items.whyNotLaw: T82's own rule - a budget names the object it measured - unclosed in the tool T82's Check sentence names. F46 fixed the LABEL in sizeBudget.mjs and the two tools now agree, which is why it reads green: they agree because both call total(), and both are low by the same 106 bytes. Gate step 17, the seat packet error and every band inherit it. Two readings. One: S21 one level down, closed the same way, by measuring what render emits. Two: the separators are a constant of the part COUNT, not content, so a cap may deliberately name content and the fix is a documented derivation, not a new number - and the prefix must stay byte-stable for the 95 per cent cache hit, so changing what is counted must not change what is emitted. Measure before ruling: whether any lane was ever issued between the two numbers, and whether D-57's 25.3 KB and D-66's 85-bytes-from-red were content or emitted bytes.

items.claim: Rule I scopes dated fields to decisions.json rows and board ledger rows - prose is not scanned. F54 put STORE_BASELINE.at in tool SOURCE dated 2026-09-23 when UTC was 2026-09-22, printed on every store run, and 22 of 22 passed.
items.whyNotLaw: Two readings the control plane cannot settle from the objects. One: extend rule I to dated fields wherever they live, F41's rule finally applied to its whole surface - the shipped tool prints (D-72, 2026-09-23) while D-72's own at is 2026-09-22, so it cites a row that contradicts it, which is rule H's family and not only a clock error. Two: a dated CONSTANT in source may be the wrong shape rather than an unchecked one. STORE_BASELINE also carries bytes 7292, files 5 and decision D-72, none tied to decisions.json, so the baseline goes stale silently and a renumbered row prints an unresolvable citation; the fix might be to derive it from the row rather than check the copy. Measure before ruling: how many dated or id-bearing constants already sit in factory/tools, and whether a check could read them without a convention that does not yet exist.
